A repository of your own, three lines about your teaching, a clone, a commit from your laptop: in about an hour.
Today we walk through the same steps together and add the part that needs a second person.
This is not a course about AI. What agents such as Claude Code do in a repository rests on exactly these steps.
Things may go wrong here. Everything we do today can be undone.

What is a commit?
A commit is a saved state of your files, with four pieces of information:

Who made it: a name and an email address
When: date and time
What changed: line by line
Why: the message you write with it

text:
From your repository into the shared one


Before

Your three lines are in your own repository teaching-your-username, in the file your-username.md
Only you write there


After

The same file is also in the shared repository workshop, in the folder people, on a branch of your own

Part 1: Create the repository (in the browser)

Open https://github.com/new while signed in.
Owner: choose gitforsci-rdc, not your own account.
Repository name: teaching- followed by your GitHub username, for example teaching-octocat.
Choose Private.
Tick Add a README file.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)
text:
Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)

In your new repository, click Add file, then Create new file.
Name the file after your GitHub username with the ending .md, for example octocat.md.
Copy these lines into the file and fill them in:
# your-username

- Who I teach:
- With which tool:
- What blocks me:
Click Commit changes…. Write the commit message Add my teaching context and click Commit changes.

A commit is one saved state of your repository, with who, when and what. You have now made your first one.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 3: Clone the repository (GitHub Desktop)
Clone a repository once. A second click on Clone makes a second copy on your laptop, and the two get mixed up.

Open GitHub Desktop. Choose the menu File, Clone Repository…, then the tab URL.
Type gitforsci-rdc/teaching- followed by your username into the first field.
Look at Local Path. It must end in gitrepos/teaching- followed by your username, in the folder gitrepos you created in Step 5.
Click Clone. GitHub Desktop shows your repository at the top left.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 4: An editor (recommended)
GitHub Desktop shows changes, but it does not edit files. I recommend Sublime Text, a free editor for plain text.

Install Sublime Text.
In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), tab Integrations, and choose Sublime Text as External Editor.

Without Sublime Text, use TextEdit on macOS or Notepad on Windows. Do not use Word.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 5: One commit from your laptop
text:
Part 5: One commit from your laptop

Open the file README.md of your repository. With Sublime Text: menu Repository, Open in Sublime Text, then click README.md. Without it: menu Repository, Show in Finder (Windows: Show in Explorer), then open README.md with TextEdit or Notepad.
Add one sentence below the title, for example what this repository is for. Save the file.
Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists README.md with a tick.
Write a commit message in the field at the bottom left, for example Describe this repository.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin at the top. Your commit is now on GitHub as well.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 6: Check and report

In GitHub Desktop, click the tab History. You see three commits: the first one made by GitHub, your three lines, and the sentence in the README.
Open your issue in the workshop repository, the one with your username in its title, and tick the box for Step 6.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Stuck?

The owner gitforsci-rdc is not in the list. The invitation is not accepted yet. Open https://github.com/orgs/gitforsci-rdc/invitation while signed in.
The push is rejected. You ticked “Block command line pushes that expose my email” in Step 4, and GitHub Desktop still uses your real address. Open Settings (Windows: File, Options), tab Git, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com and save. Then click Undo at the bottom of the tab Changes and commit again.
Something went very wrong with the clone. Delete the folder on your laptop and clone again. The version on GitHub is the latest one, as far as you pushed.
Anything else: write what you see as a comment in your issue, with a screenshot.

If this step is not finished by Friday, come anyway. You sit with a neighbour who has it, follow on their laptop and take the reviewer’s part. The educator part of the workshop needs no setup.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
To set up an account on GitHub, follow these general steps:

Go to the GitHub website at https://github.com/.
Click on the “Sign up” button on the top right corner of the page.
Enter your preferred username, email address, and password in the provided fields.
Choose whether you want to receive updates and announcements via email.
Complete the verification process by solving a puzzle and entering a verification code sent to your email.







TipUsername advice from: Happy Git and GitHub for the useR





You will be able to upgrade to a paid level of service, apply discounts, join organizations, etc. in the future, so don’t fret about any of that now. Except your username. You might want to give that some thought.
A few tips, which sadly tend to contradict each other:

Incorporate your actual name! People like to know who they’re dealing with. Also makes your username easier for people to guess or remember.
Reuse your username from other contexts, e.g., Twitter or Slack. But, of course, someone with no GitHub activity will probably be squatting on that.
Pick a username you will be comfortable revealing to your future boss.
Shorter is better than longer.
Be as unique as possible in as few characters as possible. In some settings GitHub auto-completes or suggests usernames.
Make it timeless. Don’t highlight your current university, employer, or place of residence, e.g. JennyFromTheBlock.
Avoid words laden with special meaning in programming.
Avoid the use of upper vs. lower case to separate words. We highly recommend all lowercase. GitHub treats usernames in a case insensitive way, but using all lowercase is kinder to people doing downstream regular expression work with usernames, in various languages. A better strategy for word separation is to use a hyphen -.

You can change your username later, but better to get this right the first time.

https://help.github.com/articles/changing-your-github-username/
https://help.github.com/articles/what-happens-when-i-change-my-username/




Once you have created your GitHub account, enter the username in the pre-course survey if you have not done so yet, or send it to me by email: lschoebitz@ethz.ch. I then invite you to the GitHub organisation for the course.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Thank you for joining this workshop at the Research Data Conference 2026. Your instructor Lars Schöbitz, Global Health Engineering, ETH Zurich, is looking forward to meeting you.
We meet on Friday, 20 November 2026, 09:30 to 11:30 (Europe/Zurich) in Room Wytsicht, Gurten, Bern, at the Research Data Conference 2026. Conference programme and venue: https://researchdatasupport.ch/srdsn-conference. Registration runs through the conference.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Background
Git and GitHub are the connective tissue of reproducible, collaborative research, yet many researchers learn them through fragmented tutorials that stop short of the collaboration patterns that matter: branching, pull requests, review and merging. This workshop is delivered as if every participant were a learner, and the real audience is educators: data stewards, research software engineers and instructors who teach, or want to teach, similar material. You first experience a condensed version of the full course from the learner’s seat, then switch to an educator lens to judge whether you could teach it in your own context. The course is published as an open educational resource.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Prior knowledge
No experience with Git or GitHub is assumed, and no programming. The hands-on part runs in GitHub Desktop, which works for files of any kind. In the pre-course survey some of you said you work in R, some in Python and some do not programme. If you already use Git with another tool, bring that tool.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
section: What do I need to bring to the workshop?
text:
What do I need to bring to the workshop?

a laptop with GitHub Desktop installed and its charger, connected to the conference wifi
a web browser (preferably Chrome or Firefox)
a pen and paper (we will be doing some drawings)
the pre-work below completed

Prior to the workshop, there is some pre-work for you to do. It keeps our two hours for the collaboration skills instead of setting up infrastructure.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
section: What do I need to prepare before the workshop?
text:
What do I need to prepare before the workshop?

Step 1: Complete the pre-course survey by Monday, 16 November 2026, 18:00.
Step 2: Get an account for GitHub, if you have none.
Step 3: Install GitHub Desktop and sign in.
Step 4: Decide where your email address shows.
Step 5: Do the setup check.
Step 6: Create your own repository and make your first commit.

Steps 3 to 6 take about 60 minutes and are due by Thursday, 19 November 2026, and at the latest Friday, 20 November, 09:00. The hands-on part builds on the pre-work. Anyone who arrives without it sits with a prepared neighbour, follows on their laptop and takes the reviewer’s part, and takes full part in the educator part of the workshop.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Collaboration patterns: apply the core Git and GitHub patterns, branching, pull requests, review and merging, to a small project.
Instructional design: evaluate the workshop’s design (sequencing, scaffolding, exercises) from an educator’s perspective.
Reuse: assess whether they could reuse and adapt the material to teach Git and GitHub in their own setting.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Steps

macOSWindows



Open https://desktop.github.com/ and click Download for macOS.
Open the downloaded ZIP file in your Downloads folder. Drag the program GitHub Desktop onto the Applications folder in the sidebar of the Finder.
Start GitHub Desktop. If macOS asks whether you want to open a program from the internet, click Open.
Click Sign in to GitHub.com. Your browser opens. Sign in with your GitHub account and click Authorize desktop. Allow the browser to open GitHub Desktop.
Back in GitHub Desktop you see Configure Git. Your name and email address go into every commit you make on the laptop. Under Email, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com if you do not want to show one. GitHub still links your commits to your account. Click Finish.

You are done when the menu GitHub Desktop, Settings, tab Accounts shows your GitHub username.


GitHub Desktop installs into your user folder and as a rule needs no administrator rights. If your laptop is managed and blocks the installation, ask your IT for “GitHub Desktop” and write to me so that I know.

Open https://desktop.github.com/ and click Download for Windows (64bit).
Start the downloaded file GitHubDesktopSetup-x64.exe. The installation runs without questions and opens the program at the end.
Click Sign in to GitHub.com. Your browser opens. Sign in with your GitHub account and click Authorize desktop. Allow the browser to open GitHub Desktop.
Back in GitHub Desktop you see Configure Git. Your name and email address go into every commit you make on the laptop. Under Email, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com if you do not want to show one. GitHub still links your commits to your account. Click Finish.

You are done when the menu File, Options, tab Accounts shows your GitHub username.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Stuck?

The browser does not return to the program. Close GitHub Desktop, start it again and repeat the sign-in.
You chose the wrong address under Configure Git. Open Settings (macOS) or Options (Windows), tab Git, and change it there.
Windows warns about an unknown app. Click More info, then Run anyway. The file comes from GitHub.
Anything else: write to lschoebitz@ethz.ch with a screenshot.

Next: Step 4.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Before you start: one folder for all repositories
text:
Before you start: one folder for all repositories
Create a folder named gitrepos in your Documents folder. Do not put it into a folder that syncs with iCloud, OneDrive or Dropbox. Git and the sync get in each other’s way, and changes are lost.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Steps

Accept the invitation. After you have given your GitHub username in the survey, GitHub sends you an email with the button Join @b58fc729-690b-4000-b19f-365a4093b2ff;7B7B3C2076617220636F757273652E636F6465203E7D7D;. Or open https://github.com/orgs/gitforsci-rdc/invitation while signed in.
Open GitHub Desktop. Choose the menu File, Clone Repository…, then the tab URL.
Type gitforsci-rdc/workshop into the first field.
Look at Local Path before you click anything else. Click Choose…, go to Documents, select gitrepos and confirm. The path must end in gitrepos/workshop.
Click Clone. GitHub Desktop shows Current Repository: workshop at the top left.
Open the issues of the workshop repository and click the one with your username in its title. Tick the boxes and write the comment setup complete.

You are done when your comment stands in your issue.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Stuck?

No invitation. I can only invite you once I have your username. Complete the survey and look again an hour later.
GitHub Desktop says the repository was not found. The invitation is not accepted yet, or GitHub Desktop is signed in with a different account. Check Settings or Options, tab Accounts.
The path ends in a folder named Untitled (macOS). Click Choose… again and select gitrepos without typing a name.
Anything else: write what you see as a comment in your issue, with a screenshot.

Next: Step 6.
If the setup is not finished by Friday, come anyway. You sit with a neighbour who has it, follow on their laptop and take the reviewer’s part. The educator part of the workshop needs no setup.

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
This page is the instruction for the hands-on part of the workshop. You bring the file with your three lines into the shared repository workshop, on a branch of your own and through a pull request. Your neighbour reads it and merges it.
In the workshop you work in pairs, both at the same time, each on your own laptop. Steps 1 to 5 come first. Step 6 follows after I have shown it.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Before you start
You need the finished pre-work:

the repository workshop, cloned in Step 5 to Documents/gitrepos/workshop
your own repository teaching-your-username with the file your-username.md, cloned in Step 6 to Documents/gitrepos/teaching-your-username

Is something missing? Sit with a neighbour who has it. You follow on their laptop and you are the reviewer in step 6.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 1: open the shared repository
You cloned workshop in Step 5. Do not clone it again.

Open GitHub Desktop. Click Current Repository at the top left and choose workshop.
Click Fetch origin at the top. If the button then reads Pull origin, click it once more. Your copy now has the latest state of main.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 2: create a branch
A branch is a line of work of your own in the shared repository. You can add files on it without touching main.

Click Current Branch at the top, then New Branch.
As the name, write people- followed by your GitHub username, for example people-octocat. Click Create Branch.
The top now reads Current Branch: people-your-username.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 3: copy your file
You copy the one file with your three lines from your own repository into the shared one. Your own repository stays as it is.
Copy the file, never the whole folder teaching-your-username. The folder carries a hidden folder named .git, and Git would then see a repository inside a repository.

macOSWindows



In Finder, open Documents/gitrepos/teaching-your-username.
Click the file your-username.md once and press Command and C.
Open Documents/gitrepos/workshop/people and press Command and V.




In Explorer, open Documents\gitrepos\teaching-your-username.
Click the file your-username.md once and press Ctrl and C.
Open Documents\gitrepos\workshop\people and press Ctrl and V.




The folder people now holds _example.md and your file.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 4: commit

Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists people/your-username.md with a tick.
Write a message in the field Summary at the bottom left, for example Add my teaching context.
The button below now reads Commit 1 file to people-your-username. If it ends in to main, you are on the wrong branch. Go back to step 2.
Click the button.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
section: Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
text:
Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
Your branch exists only on your laptop so far.

Click Publish branch at the top. GitHub Desktop pushes the branch with your commit to GitHub.
Click the blue button Preview Pull Request. A window shows your file.
At the top it reads base: main and compare: people-your-username. That is how it should be. Click Create Pull Request at the bottom right. Your browser opens on github.com.
The text field holds a template with two lines. Fill in File with people/your-username.md.
On the right, click Reviewers and type the username of your neighbour. Choose them from the list.
Click the green button Create pull request.

Your pull request is open. Do not merge it yourself, also when GitHub shows you the button. Reading by a second person is the point of the exercise.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 6: review, answer, merge
Each of you is the author of one pull request and the reviewer of the other.

Reviewer: open the pull requests of the workshop repository and click your neighbour’s. Click the tab Files changed. Move the mouse over the line What blocks me, click the blue plus sign, write one question and click Add single comment.
Author: you see the comment in your pull request. Answer it in the file: open Documents/gitrepos/workshop/people/your-username.md in your editor, change the line and save. In GitHub Desktop, write a commit message, click Commit 1 file to people-your-username, then Push origin. The open pull request shows the new commit. You need no second pull request.
Reviewer: go back to the tab Conversation, click Merge pull request, then Confirm merge.
Both: in GitHub Desktop, click Current Branch and choose main. Click Fetch origin, then Pull origin. The folder people on your laptop now holds the files of everyone who is merged.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Done when
Your pull request stands under closed pull requests with the purple mark Merged, and your file is in the folder people on main.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Stuck?

A commit on main instead of your branch. As long as you have not pushed, GitHub Desktop shows the button Undo at the bottom left, below the commit. Click it. Then create the branch (step 2). GitHub Desktop asks whether your changes should come along. Choose to bring them to the new branch.
Nothing appears in the tab Changes. The file is in a different place. It belongs into gitrepos/workshop/people.
Changes shows a folder instead of one file. You copied the repository folder. Delete the copied folder from workshop/people and copy only the file your-username.md.
The push is rejected. Your commit carries your real email address, and your account blocks such pushes. In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), Git, tab Author, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com and click Save. Then click Undo at the bottom of the tab Changes and commit again.
Publish branch is missing, the top reads Push origin. The branch is published already. Click Push origin if commits are missing and go on with step 5.
Your neighbour is not in the list of reviewers. They have not accepted the invitation to the organisation. Go on without a reviewer and tell them the number of your pull request.
Anything else: raise your hand in the workshop, or write a comment in your issue in the workshop repository.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request
